prize_parts.citation: for discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1, its active peptide form and its receptor-mediated physiological actions, which enabled glucose-dependent therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: a single part, B035, for Holst, Drucker and Mojsov. The first-round exchange did not weaken the scientific case, and the chair's summary confirms that no member raises a maturity objection to the discovery itself. What it did show is that the remaining disagreement is about attribution and framing, not merit. The discovery chain is separable into three steps that each carry independent weight: the incretin effect and the physiology of GLP-1 (Holst), proglucagon biology and receptor action (Drucker), and identification of the biologically active truncated peptide (Mojsov). Each has been confirmed repeatedly by independent groups and trials, and the downstream effects on glycaemia, body weight and cardiovascular and renal outcomes are large and well documented. A citation written around the hormone, its active form and its actions keeps the prize a discovery prize and makes the three-name set coherent. Industrial development, including Knudsen's long-acting analogues, is acknowledged in the narrative rather than the credited names.
statement.case_against: Credit remains the weak point and I do not think round 1 resolved it. Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) form relative to Habener and colleagues, who are outside the credited list, is described as contested by all six of us, and none of us has evidence in the supplied record that settles it. The three-name limit excludes Knudsen, whose acylated analogues turned the biology into practical drugs, so a discovery-framed prize can be read as omitting the step that delivered patient benefit. If the committee decides the therapeutic step is the prize-worthy innovation, my trio is the wrong set. Long-term safety and durability of obesity treatment are still accruing, though they do not bear on the discovery.

responses.point: If Knudsen must be included, the cost should fall on Mojsov and not on Holst, whose incretin physiology is the longest-standing foundation; the citation should be built around physiology and the active peptide so that omitting the drug developer is coherent.
responses.response: I agree with the citation logic and have adopted it: with a physiology and active-peptide framing, Knudsen's exclusion is a principled consequence of the discovery criterion and not an oversight. I also agree Holst should be the last name to go. Where I would add a caution is that the same logic cuts against Mojsov only if her step is judged redundant to Holst's and Drucker's work, and I do not think it is. Physiology of the incretin effect and receptor biology do not by themselves identify which peptide form is active, so removing her leaves a gap in the chain. If her priority is shown to be weaker than the committee currently assumes, I would then accept the substitution you describe, but I would not make it on the strength of an unresolved dispute.

responses.point: Sandberg would accept Knudsen in place of Mojsov if the evidence for Mojsov's priority proves weaker than he judges it, and would pair B035 with a June and Sadelain part from B029 if the committee wanted two achievements, at the cost of dropping Mojsov or Holst.
responses.response: I share your conditional on Mojsov and treat it as the real hinge of this configuration. I part from you on the two-part option. Because B035 already uses all three names, pairing it with B029 would force a cut from the strongest case to make room for one whose own credit is incomplete, given the missing early chimeric-receptor concept. That trade weakens both parts. I would prefer one coherent achievement with an uncontested maturity record to two parts, one of which has an unresolved attribution gap. We also now differ slightly less on Knudsen than in round 1: I accept that her inclusion is defensible if the committee reframes the prize around the therapy, but then the whole citation changes and the choice of which academic discoverer to drop becomes the central question, which I would not want to settle by default.

responses.point: Perlmann asks that the secretariat verify the historical record on the active GLP-1 peptide, Mojsov versus Habener-group contributions, before the final ballot, since a mistake would be hard to defend.
responses.response: I agree and would make this the one condition on my vote. My round-1 uncertainty was the same, and the chair's questions show that none of us can settle it from what we have been given. I also agree with your reading that identification of the 7-36 form and its insulinotropic activity is complementary to Holst and Drucker, not duplicative. My position is therefore conditional but stable: I vote for the trio as it stands, and if verified evidence showed Mojsov's contribution to be materially secondary to earlier work by someone outside the list, I would reconsider the third name instead of the framing.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius holds Knudsen's exclusion with less confidence than Perlmann and wants the citation to acknowledge the therapeutic consequence; she would not lightly drop Rosenberg from B029 because adoptive transfer of gene-engineered T cells belongs to the same lineage.
responses.response: I have taken your point about the therapeutic consequence into the citation by ending it on the glucose-dependent therapies for type 2 diabetes and obesity, which names the outcome without crediting a product. That is the most we can do within three names and a discovery criterion. On B029, I take your argument about Rosenberg seriously and no longer think narrowing to June and Sadelain is as simple as I implied in round 1. Even so, the omission of Eshhar's original concept remains an attribution gap that no choice among the three credited names can repair, and that is why I keep B029 as my first alternative and not as a second part.

responses.point: El-Manira keeps optogenetics (B046) as an alternative, noting that dropping Boyden, Bamberg and Miesenbock to fit three slots is arbitrary and that Deisseroth, Nagel and Hegemann is a judgement call.
responses.response: I agree, and I will not defend B046 by field affinity, as I too work in a neighbouring area. Your point that the discovery of channelrhodopsins as light-gated channels is distinct from the neuronal implementation sharpens my own concern: any trio splits one story in two. The impact on medicine is so far mainly as a research tool. I keep it as my second alternative, with no change in its position since round 1.

uncertainties: Whether the documentary record supports Mojsov's priority for the active GLP-1(7-36) form relative to Habener and colleagues; I cannot resolve this from the supplied material and it is the one point that could change my third name.
Whether the committee will frame the citation around physiology and the active peptide or around the therapeutic step, which would require Knudsen to displace one of the three academic discoverers.
Whether B029 could be configured cleanly enough, given the missing original chimeric-receptor concept and the Rosenberg question, to serve as a second part, which I currently judge it cannot.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict is apparent for B035, B029 or B046 and I know of no documented tie to Drucker, Holst, Mojsov, Knudsen or the other credited names. I continue to disclose my co-authorship with Rickard Sandberg (eight co-authored works per the profile record, not independently audited) and my co-authorship of the 2016 spatial transcriptomics paper, which concern research outside the shortlisted ballots. I would reconsider and disclose again if the shortlist changed.
